sentences.text: The extinct animal known as Eremopezus contains only one verified species, Eremopezus eocaenus.
This was a gigantic, likely flightless bird with well-known legs extending from the lower leg to the midfoot and a somewhat ponderous body size similar to Mullerornis betsilei.
The genus name translates to 'walking hermit,' derived from Greek words for a solitary place and walking.

It possessed widely divergent toes capable of flexing through a wide range of positions, supported by strong tendons that provided a firm grip, and a tarsometatarsus with a small hypotarsus featuring a single simple crest and lacking foramina for tendons.
Its feathers were likely white, black, or grey, containing eumelanin but little carotenoids and phaeomelanins, which is typical of higher waterbirds in similar habitats.
No known palaeognaths evolved gripping feet like Eremopezus, nor did they thrive in wetland habitats like those in the Jebel Qatrani Formation.
Researchers suggest Eremopezus behaved similarly to secretarybirds and shoebills in the swamps of the Jebel Qatrani Formation.
The genus and species were both described by C. W. Andrews in 1904.
The original description was based on a distal left tibiotarsus specimen.

Fossils were found in the Upper Eocene Jebel Qatrani Formation near the Qasr el Sagha escarpment, north of Lake Birket Qarun near Faiyum in Egypt, and were previously thought to be from the Early Oligocene but this is now considered incorrect.

Piscivory or generalist predation are plausible diets for Eremopezus given its habitat, although many flightless birds are herbivorous or omnivorous. It is hypothesized that E. eocaenus might have been a frugivore or herbivore of swamp forests, though early Neoaves are generally predatory. As a predator, it likely fed mainly on mid-sized terrestrial vertebrates such as large reptiles or small mammals.
Unmated birds were probably solitary.
Fossils date from a time when the region had more forest and less grassland than it did six million years later, and the habitat likely resembled the modern Niger Delta.

Researchers initially believed Eremopezus was a ratite closely related to the elephant birds of Madagascar, but the presence of deep ligamental pits on the distal condyles distinguishes it from elephant birds, and its tarsometatarsus resembles that of general ratites like emus or ostriches rather than elephant birds.

It is debated whether Eremopezus represents a separate example of ratite bodyplan origins or is a flightless neognath, and it may belong to a distinct family, Eremopezidae, because its closest relatives are unknown.

Fossils of Eremopezus date to the Late Eocene epoch, found in rocks deposited between approximately 36 and 33 million years ago, specifically in the Priabonian stage with the oldest dating to about 36 million years ago and the youngest to no less than 33 million years ago.
The time range is from the Priabonian to the Rupelian, between 37.71 and 27.3 million years ago.
There is a debate regarding whether certain fossil eggshells from the Maghreb belong to Eremopezus or to ostriches.
It is debated whether Eremopezus possessed a hook or 'nail' on its bill tip if it was a pelecaniform, and robust conclusions about its habits remain impossible without further fossil data.
It is debated whether flightless birds can compete with carnivorous mammals, as the Phorusrhacidae prove that carnivorous flightless birds can thrive alongside mammalian competitors.
